nodes.label: Special Duty Categories
nodes.summary: Special categories where the duty of care is either restricted or expanded: pure economic loss, negligent misstatement, psychiatric injury, omissions, product liability, and public authority duty.

nodes.label: Pure Economic Loss
nodes.summary: Generally no duty of care for pure economic loss in negligence (not consequential to physical damage). Exceptions exist for negligent misstatement, assumption of responsibility, and certain relational loss categories.

nodes.label: Negligent Misstatement
nodes.summary: Liability for careless words causing economic loss arises where there is an assumption of responsibility, special relationship of skill/knowledge, and reasonable reliance by the claimant.

nodes.label: Assumption of Responsibility
nodes.summary: A duty may arise where the defendant expressly or impliedly assumes responsibility to the claimant, creating a special relationship akin to a contractual undertaking.

nodes.label: Professional Adviser Duty
nodes.summary: Professionals (solicitors, accountants, surveyors) owe a duty of care to clients in contract and tort. Liability to third parties depends on assumption of responsibility and reasonable reliance.

nodes.label: Product Liability (Common Law)
nodes.summary: Manufacturers owe a duty of care to consumers for defective products under Donoghue v Stevenson. HK also has statutory consumer protection (Sale of Goods Ordinance, Consumer Goods Safety Ordinance).

nodes.label: Psychiatric Injury Overview
nodes.summary: Nervous shock / psychiatric harm: duty is restricted by policy considerations. Distinction between primary victims (participants in event) and secondary victims (witnesses). HK approach needs verification.

nodes.label: Psychiatric Injury: Primary Victims
nodes.summary: A primary victim is within the zone of foreseeable physical danger. Duty is owed if psychiatric injury is a foreseeable consequence of the defendant's breach.

nodes.label: Psychiatric Injury: Secondary Victims (Alcock Control Mechanisms)
nodes.summary: Secondary victims must satisfy: close tie of love and affection, proximity to the event, and witnessing the aftermath through own unaided senses (Alcock criteria).

nodes.label: Psychiatric Injury: Rescuers
nodes.summary: Rescuers may be treated as primary or secondary victims depending on whether they are within the zone of physical danger. Policy favouring rescuers in psychiatric injury claims.

nodes.label: Omissions and Duty to Control Third Parties
nodes.summary: No general duty to act to prevent harm to another. Exceptions: assumption of responsibility, control over a dangerous thing or third party, statutory duty, or special relationship (parent/child, employer/employee).

nodes.label: Public Authority Duty
nodes.summary: Public authorities may owe a duty of care in negligence where policy decisions (immune) are distinguished from operational decisions (duty may arise). HK position requires verification.

nodes.label: Rescuers
nodes.summary: A duty of care is owed to rescuers who suffer injury while attempting to rescue someone endangered by the defendant's negligence. Foreseeability of rescue is key.

nodes.label: Unborn Children, Wrongful Life and Parental Autonomy
nodes.summary: HK position on prenatal injury, wrongful life claims by disabled children, and parental autonomy in medical decisions requires verification. UK and Commonwealth authorities as persuasive guides.

nodes.label: Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd [1964] AC 465
nodes.summary: Negligent misstatement liability: assumption of responsibility and reasonable reliance. Key authority for pure economic loss in negligence.

nodes.label: Tai Hing Cotton Mill Ltd v Liu Chong Hing Bank Ltd [1986] AC 80
nodes.summary: PC case on economic loss: no duty of care for pure economic loss in banking context unless assumption of responsibility.

nodes.label: Yuen Kun Yeu v Attorney General of Hong Kong [1988] AC 175
nodes.summary: PC case on public authority duty and economic loss. No duty owed by regulator to depositors.

nodes.label: Cheng Yuen v Royal Hongkong Jockey Club [1993] HKCFI 89
nodes.summary: Seed case for negligent misstatement / assumption of responsibility in HK. Needs paragraph verification.

nodes.label: Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire [1992] 1 AC 310
nodes.summary: Secondary victim psychiatric injury: must satisfy close tie, proximity, and witnessing through own senses. Hillsborough disaster.

nodes.label: McLoughlin v O'Brian [1983] 1 AC 410
nodes.summary: Secondary victim: witnessing immediate aftermath of accident sufficient; proximity in time and space required.

nodes.label: Page v Smith [1996] AC 155
nodes.summary: Primary victim: duty owed for psychiatric injury where physical injury was foreseeable, even if psychiatric injury was not itself foreseeable.

nodes.label: Chu Siu Kuk Yuen v Jockey Club [1994] HKCFI 234
nodes.summary: Seed case for psychiatric injury / nervous shock in HK. Needs paragraph verification.

nodes.label: Lau Luen Hung v Commissioner of Police [2009] HKCFI 678
nodes.summary: Seed case for public authority duty / police negligence in HK. Needs paragraph verification.

nodes.label: Verify HK Pure Economic Loss Leading Cases
nodes.summary: Research and verify HK CFA / CA decisions on pure economic loss in negligence. Identify whether incremental approach or three-stage test is preferred.

nodes.label: Verify HK Psychiatric Injury Leading Cases
nodes.summary: Research and verify HK decisions on primary/secondary victim distinction and Alcock control mechanisms in HK.
